evidence.text: Instagram Ranking Explained | How Our Algorithm Works | About Instagram Instagram Ranking Explained By Adam Mosseri May 31, 2023 We want to do a better job of explaining how Instagram works. There are a lot of misconceptions out there, and we recognize that we can do more to help people, especially creators, understand what we do. Today, we’re updating our original post to shed more light on how ranking works across Instagram and share some new features we’ve built in response to feedback from creators that help improve the experiences people have across the app overall. Ranking on Instagram We want to share more on how ranking works across Instagram to help people maximize their experience and help creators understand how their content might be surfaced. Instagram doesn’t have a singular algorithm that oversees what people do and don’t see on the app. We use a variety of algorithms, classifiers, and processes, each with its own purpose. We want to make the most of people’s time, and we believe that using technology to personalize everyone’s experience is the best way to do that. Each part of the app – Feed, Stories, Explore, Reels, Search and more – uses its own algorithm tailored to how people use it. People tend to look for their closest friends in Stories, use Explore to discover new content and creators and be entertained in Reels. We rank things differently in these different parts of the app, and have added features and controls like Close Friends, Favorites and Following so you can further customize your experience. How we rank Feed Feed is your personalized home base within Instagram to help you catch up with friends, family, and interests. This means your feed will have a mix of content from the accounts you’ve chosen to follow, recommended content from accounts we think you’ll enjoy and ads. You’ll also see a mixture of videos, photos and carousels. With any ranking algorithm, how it works can be broken down into steps. We start by defining the set of things we plan to rank in the first place. With Feed we consider recent posts shared by the people you follow, as well as posts from accounts you don’t already follow that we think you might be interested in. We determine what you might be interested in based on a variety of factors, including what and whom you’ve followed, liked or engaged with recently. We personalize the experience for you to try to strike a balance between content from accounts you follow with content from accounts you don’t follow but might be interested in. Next we take all the information we have about what was posted, the people who made those posts, and your preferences. We’ve also started considering other factors like format, so if we notice you prefer photos, we’ll show you more photos. We call these “signals,” and there are thousands of them. They include everything from when a post was shared to whether you’re using a phone or the web to how often you like videos. The most important signals across Feed, roughly in order of importance, are: Your activity. Posts you’ve liked, shared, saved or commented on help us understand what you might be interested in. Information about the post. These are signals both about how popular a post is – think how many people have liked it and how quickly people are liking, commenting, sharing and saving a post – and more mundane information about the content itself, like when it was posted, and what location, if any, was attached to it. Information about the person who posted. This helps us get a sense for how interesting the person might be to you, and includes signals like how many times people have interacted with that person in the past few weeks. Your history of interacting with someone. This gives us a sense of how interested you are generally in seeing posts from a particular person. An example is whether or not you comment on each other’s posts. From there we make a set of predictions. These are educated guesses at how likely you are to interact with

evidence.label: Launch brief
evidence.text:
Launch brief

Somebody has launched, but the page is not converting well.

What we know: signup conversion is weak, and many visitors do not immediately recognise that Somebody is built for founders running very small companies or understand how it differs from other AI tools.

The current page leans on broad "AI manager" and "automate your workflows" language. We suspect the positioning is too generic, but we do not yet have strong evidence for the words founders themselves use to describe the problem.

Prepare a stronger relaunch message for review today. Do not publish or send anything yet.

evidence.label: Company profile
evidence.text:
About Somebody

Somebody is an AI manager for founders running one-person companies and lean teams. It is designed to take responsibility for moving an objective forward: organising work inside the company, bringing in outside help when needed, and staying with the job until there is a usable result.

The product is for founders who personally carry several parts of the business and need important work to keep moving without adding another tool to manage.

Positioning should stay practical and outcome-focused. Do not imply that Somebody replaces the founder or guarantees a business result.

evidence.label: Partnership evaluation criteria
evidence.text:
Partnership evaluation criteria (internal):
1. Relevance: the target must serve SME / one-person-company buyers with a product the company can resell, refer or integrate.
2. Reliability: publicly verifiable operating history of at least 12 months, or a credible parent organisation.
3. Reachability: an identified business contact channel (public business email or partner form).
4. Risk posture: no unresolved public fraud/sanction signals; clear terms of service.
5. Economics: free tier, referral or partner programme preferred over paid-only access.

Objective deliverable

Founder-facing marketing plan - review draft only
Status: Draft for founder review. Do not publish or send yet.

Evidence base
- Company profile (company/profile): Somebody is an AI manager for founders running one-person companies and lean teams. It organises work, brings in outside help when needed, and stays with an objective until there is a usable result. Positioning should be practical and outcome-focused; do not imply replacement of the founder or guaranteed results.
- Launch brief (launch/context): signup conversion is weak; many visitors do not recognise the target audience or how the product differs from other AI tools. Current language is broad, and strong evidence for founders' own problem wording is not yet available.

Core relaunch message
Somebody helps founders running one-person companies and lean teams keep important work moving by organising the work, bringing in help when needed, and staying with the objective through a usable result. Lead with the founder and practical outcome. Avoid replacement or guaranteed-result claims.

Audience and message alignment
Primary audience: founders running one-person companies and lean teams, especially those personally carrying several business functions.
Evidence-based problem: important work needs to keep moving without adding another tool to manage; visitors may not recognise the audience or differentiation.
Message job: make the audience and practical role clear, then show how Somebody stays with an objective rather than using generic AI language.
CTA: not specified in the records; propose only after review of destination and wording.

Channel plan
TikTok - provisional discovery/testing. Show a founder multi-role workload and the keep-an-objective-moving promise in short demonstrations.
Instagram - provisional core launch storytelling. Use visual explainers and product stories so one-person-company and lean-team founders recognise themselves and understand the difference from generic AI tools.
Facebook - provisional targeted explanation and community reuse. Provide accessible context and detail using approved assets.
X - provisional message testing and founder conversation. Test concise practical positioning and invite discussion.
All channel content must use an audience qualifier, practical outcome framing, evidence-safe CTAs, and no unsupported guarantees. These roles and priorities are hypotheses, not measured channel results.

Provisional launch-week timing
No exact relaunch date is recorded. Before the week: review message, destination, CTA, claims, creative capacity, and measurement plan. Day 1: approved explainer on Instagram and X. Day 2: TikTok founder scenario adapted for Instagram Reels. Day 3: Facebook explanation and X question. Day 4: second TikTok/Instagram scenario. Day 5: compare channel-level attention and signup signals and select the strongest evidence-safe message. Days 6-7: repeat the best approved format, document learnings, and prepare founder review. Planning only; no posting or sending is authorized.

Prioritization
Clarify audience and product difference because weak signup conversion and audience/differentiation confusion are evidenced problems. Provisionally start with Instagram and X for the message system, TikTok for scenario tests, and Facebook for detail/context. Reuse one approved message across channels. Review qualitative responses and signup results before adding effort or budget. No budget, capacity, success target, or baseline is recorded.

Measurement, target interpretation, and launch-week decisions
Evidence versus assumptions:
- Evidence: launch/context reports weak signup conversion, unclear audience and differentiation, broad current language, and no strong evidence for founder wording. Company/profile defines the audience and practical product role.
- Assumption: the provisional channel roles and priorities may be useful tests; no channel-performance evidence establishes superiority.
- Assumption: clearer audience-and-role wording may improve understanding and signup behaviour; proposed wording is a test, not validated customer language.

Success indicators:
1. Signup conversion rate by channel and message/format: signups divided by attributable visits. Interpret against a supplied pre-launch baseline; without a baseline or numeric target, make no pass/fail claim.
2. Attributable visits by channel and message/format: visits assigned to an approved launch item. Use for comparison only where tracking is equivalent; it is not product-market-fit evidence by itself.
3. Audience recognition: count and proportion of reviewed responses identifying Somebody as for founders running one-person companies or lean teams. Treat as a research signal and do not generalise from an unspecified sample.
4. Differentiation comprehension: count and proportion of reviewed responses describing the practical role rather than generic AI language. Compare variants descriptively; no target is recorded.
5. Qualitative themes: code approved feedback with source, date, channel, and message variant. Use to refine wording only after review; do not infer prevalence without a defined sample and method.

Target status and decision rules
No numeric baseline, target, sample size, attribution method, exact relaunch date, or owner is recorded. These are gaps, not values to infer. Before publication or sending, the founder should approve the baseline window, numeric targets, tracking method, response-review method, and owner. At Day 5, select a message/format for Days 6-7 only if measurement is available and it is directionally stronger on the agreed signup and comprehension indicators; the founder must define directionally stronger. If tracking is unavailable, responses are insufficiently reviewed, or comparison is unfair, do not declare a winner or add effort/budget. If a message is weaker, pause repetition and review audience label, differentiation explanation, destination, and CTA before changing channel priority. Do not infer causality from untracked or confounded comparisons. Results inform only the next approved message/format iteration and review decision; they do not authorise publishing, sending, budget, or channel expansion.

Assumptions and gaps
A one-week sequence is assumed; exact date is missing. Channel account ownership, audience size, capacity, format constraints, quantified objective, baseline, comparison window, attribution, sample and coding method, budget, owner, CTA, destination, assets, cadence, audience research, validated wording, and evidence of channel/message improvement are missing. Confirm through company records or research; do not infer.

Review decision requested
Approve or revise the core message, channel roles, timing, CTA/destination, owners, budget/capacity, measurement definitions, baseline, numeric targets, attribution, qualitative review method, and decision rules before publication or sending.

Message job: make the audience and practical role immediately clear, then show how Somebody stays with an objective rather than using broad generic AI language.

Channel plan

TikTok — Priority: provisional discovery/testing.
Role: Make the founder’s multi-role workload and the “keep an objective moving” promise concrete in short demonstrations.
Audience/message: speak to founders doing many jobs; show organising, bringing in outside help, and follow-through without implying founder replacement.
Content requirements: short vertical video; one founder scenario; problem-to-result narrative; workflow demonstration or screen recording; audience qualifier; evidence-safe CTA; no generic automation claims.

Instagram — Priority: provisional core launch storytelling.
Role: Turn the relaunch message into repeatable visual explainers and product stories.
Audience/message: help one-person-company and lean-team founders recognise themselves and understand the difference from generic AI tools.
Content requirements: Reels or carousels; specific founder situation; “how Somebody helps” steps; practical outcome framing; consistent audience label; caption explaining usable-result orientation; no unsupported guarantees.

Facebook — Priority: provisional targeted explanation and community reuse.
Role: Provide accessible context and more detail while reusing approved relaunch assets.
Audience/message: explain the product practically for founders carrying multiple business functions.
Content requirements: concise launch post; explanatory visual or short video; audience qualifier; product-difference explanation; link/CTA only after destination and wording approval. Do not assume a group, demographic, or paid audience without evidence.

X — Priority: provisional message testing and founder conversation.
Role: Test concise positioning language and invite discussion about keeping important work moving.
Audience/message: direct practical language for founders and lean teams; contrast Somebody’s specific role with generic AI framing without unsupported claims.
Content requirements: concise positioning post/thread; one workflow example; audience qualifier; reply prompts for qualitative learning; review-approved CTA. Responses are research signals, not validated customer language until reviewed.

Provisional launch-week timing
No exact relaunch date is recorded. Before the week: review message, landing-page destination, CTA, claims, creative capacity, and measurement plan. Day 1: approved audience-and-role explainer on Instagram and X. Day 2: TikTok founder-scenario demonstration adapted for Instagram Reels. Day 3: Facebook explanatory post and X question for qualitative learning. Day 4: second TikTok/Instagram scenario focused on staying with an objective through a usable result. Day 5: compare channel-level attention and signup signals and select the strongest evidence-safe message. Days 6–7: repeat the best approved format, document learnings, and prepare founder review. This is planning only; no posting or sending is authorized.

Prioritization
1. Clarify audience and product difference on the landing page and in the core message because weak signup conversion and audience/differentiation confusion are evidenced problems.
2. Provisionally start with Instagram and X for the message system, TikTok for scenario tests, and Facebook for detail/context. This is a hypothesis, not a measured channel result.
3. Reuse one approved message across all four channels, adapting format rather than inventing unsupported promises.
4. Review qualitative responses and signup results before adding effort or budget. No budget, staffing capacity, success target, or baseline is recorded.

Assumptions and gaps
- A one-week sequence is assumed for planning; exact relaunch date is missing.
- It is assumed all four channels and formats are available; account ownership, audience size, capacity, and format constraints are missing.
- The priority ranking is a working hypothesis without channel performance evidence.
- Missing: quantified objective and target, budget, owner/capacity, CTA and destination, creative assets, cadence, audience research, validated customer wording, and evidence of which channel/message improves conversion.
- Confirm these items through company records or research; do not infer them.

Review decision requested
Approve or revise the core message, channel roles, provisional priority, timing, CTA/destination, owners, budget/capacity, and success metric before publication or sending.

Review qualitative responses and signup results before adding effort or budget. No budget, capacity, success target, or baseline is recorded.

Measurement, target interpretation, and launch-week decisions
Evidence versus assumptions:
- Evidence: launch/context reports weak signup conversion, unclear audience and differentiation, broad current language, and no strong evidence for founder wording. Company/profile defines the audience and practical product role.
- Assumption: the provisional channel roles and priorities may be useful tests; no channel-performance evidence establishes superiority.
- Assumption: clearer audience-and-role wording may improve understanding and signup behaviour; proposed wording is a test, not validated customer language.

Success indicators:
1. Signup conversion rate by channel and message/format: signups divided by attributable visits. Interpret against a supplied pre-launch baseline; without a baseline or numeric target, make no pass/fail claim.
2. Attributable visits by channel and message/format: visits assigned to an approved launch item. Use for comparison only where tracking is equivalent; it is not product-market-fit evidence by itself.
3. Audience recognition: count and proportion of reviewed responses identifying Somebody as for founders running one-person companies or lean teams. Treat as a research signal and do not generalise from an unspecified sample.
4. Differentiation comprehension: count and proportion of reviewed responses describing the practical role rather than generic AI language. Compare variants descriptively; no target is recorded.
5. Qualitative themes: code approved feedback with source, date, channel, and message variant. Use to refine wording only after review; do not infer prevalence without a defined sample and method.

Target status and decision rules
No numeric baseline, target, sample size, attribution method, exact relaunch date, or owner is recorded. These are gaps, not values to infer. Before publication or sending, the founder should approve the baseline window, numeric targets, tracking method, response-review method, and owner. At Day 5, select a message/format for Days 6-7 only if measurement is available and it is directionally stronger on the agreed signup and comprehension indicators; the founder must define directionally stronger. If tracking is unavailable, responses are insufficiently reviewed, or comparison is unfair, do not declare a winner or add effort/budget. If a message is weaker, pause repetition and review audience label, differentiation explanation, destination, and CTA before changing channel priority. Do not infer causality from untracked or confounded comparisons. Results inform only the next approved message/format iteration and review decision; they do not authorise publishing, sending, budget, or channel expansion.

Assumptions and gaps
A one-week sequence is assumed; exact date is missing. Channel account ownership, audience size, capacity, format constraints, quantified objective, baseline, comparison window, attribution, sample and coding method, budget, owner, CTA, destination, assets, cadence, audience research, validated wording, and evidence of channel/message improvement are missing. Confirm through company records or research; do not infer.

Review decision requested
Approve or revise the core message, channel roles, timing, CTA/destination, owners, budget/capacity, measurement definitions, baseline, numeric targets, attribution, qualitative review method, and decision rules before publication or sending.
